deep.reconstruction: Context: Fermat's problem of finding a prime larger than any given number. On the previous page Euler recalls that 2^32+1 = 641·6700417 refutes Fermat's conjecture that every 2^(2^n)+1 is prime. On this page he argues that no formula could reliably generate only primes. Even if a formula produced a hundred primes, one could not trust it beyond that without a proof. He then proves a theorem. Theorem: no 'algebraic progression' (a sequence whose x-th term is a polynomial X(x) = α + βx + γx² + ...) has only prime terms. Proof: take any index a with value A = X(a). For x = nA + a, every term γ(nA+a)^k is congruent to γa^k mod A. Hence X(nA+a) ≡ X(a) = A ≡ 0 (mod A). So the infinitely many terms with indices nA+a are divisible by A, and are not prime once they exceed A. He then relaxes the requirement: it would suffice to have a progression containing infinitely many primes whose indices are recognisable. The example he begins (completed on the next page) is f(p) prime whenever p is prime, i.e. a rule producing a new prime from any given prime. He judges this hopeless.
errors: Euler does not state that the coefficients must be integers. With merely rational coefficients giving integer values (e.g. x(x+1)/2 + c) the congruence X(nA+a) ≡ X(a) mod A can fail. The argument then needs repair, e.g. by clearing denominators: take x = a + nDA, where D is a common denominator.

Also tacit: the polynomial is nonconstant, |A| > 1, and X(nA+a) ≠ ±A. A nonconstant polynomial takes each value only finitely often, so all but finitely many of the terms are proper multiples of A, hence composite. Euler's word 'infiniti' covers this, but it is not argued.
The 'etc.' could suggest infinite power series. The argument is valid only for polynomials (finitely many terms).

ideas.what: No nonconstant integer polynomial takes only prime values, via f(a + nf(a)) ≡ 0 mod f(a)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Christian Goldbach (letter to Euler, 1752); Euler; later restated by Legendre

ideas.what: Weaker requirement: a function sending primes to primes (a rule generating a new prime from any given prime)
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore; later prime-representing functions such as Mills (1947)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the classical, well-known Goldbach/Euler argument, widely cited in the histories (e.g. Dickson's History, Vol. I). Nothing on this page is uncredited or novel.
